import.inKnowledge: in Knowledge (knowledge base → More → Import and export)

typeSays.items: list of objects with the fields:

describe.places: Other places: "s. 23", "nr 24", "rozdz. 4" (page, number, chapter — written this way); in a recording — the time: "1:23", "1:23–1:45", "1:02:03".
describe.bible: Write a place in Holy Scripture (a reference to a work with "workType": "bible" — in a quote's "locator", in a text's footnote, in a field with a place in Knowledge) together with the book: Dz 1,14 · Dz 1,14-16 · Łk 1,26–2,5 · Dz 1,8.14 · Ps 23 · Mt 5,3-12; 6,1. Books may be in Polish (BT), Latin (Nova Vulgata) or English (Acts 1:14) — the app recognises them, orders quotes in the order of the Bible and finds everything that points to a given verse, in all translations.
describe.markup:
## Content markup (fields "body" and "further" of a text, plan points "plan[].text", "transcript" and "added[].text" of a delivery)
  ## Subheading            (# or ## — subheading, ### — smaller)
  An empty line separates paragraphs; a single line break stays (psalms, hymns).
  **bold**  *italic*  [link text](https://…)
  [@key]                   reference to a source (work, quote, person) — becomes a footnote
  [@key, s. 23]            with a place in the source
  [@bt, J 6,35; @key2]     several references in one footnote
  [@text-key]              reference to an OWN entry (text, project, knowledge-base entry — e.g. a comment) — never a footnote: in the text it becomes a link “(see its title)”
  [[these words|@key]]     link to an entry with your own words (e.g. [[sermon on bread|@kazanie-chleb]]) — also never a footnote
  ^[footnote text]         your own footnote, without a source
  ![@quote-key]            a quote from the library as a separate block, captioned with where it comes from
  ![@entry-id]             a knowledge-base entry with block content (e.g. a comment) as a separate block — whole, with tables
  [[house|@id-słowa]]      link to a knowledge-base entry (e.g. a word from a dictionary) — the reader sees it if they may read that base
  ![@id-widoku]            a knowledge-base view as a separate block (e.g. in a plan point): a list that changes together with the data — e.g. “psalms of Sunday Lauds” from the psalter
  > text                   indented quote
  - item   ·   1. item
  ---                      separating line
  \sign                    a sign without meaning (e.g. \* instead of italics)
Footnotes number themselves; the first time a source is given in full, then shortened with “op. cit.”, and right after itself — “Ibid.”. A bibliography appears below the text.
{bible}
A source (what came from outside) is cited, your own entries are linked: [@ratzinger2007, s. 183; @kazanie-chleb] gives a footnote to the book and in the text a link “(see Bread of Life)”. What the reader cannot open shows as “[reference unavailable]” (or just the words from [[…|@…]]) — without a title and without a key.
A key is a help while writing: the app remembers a fixed link to the entry (its id), so a later change of the key does not break the text. Instead of a key you can also give the entry's id: [@01a1…-…, s. 3]. A key that does not exist stays in the text as it is (with a warning at import).
describe.head:
# Library as JSON ("{format}", version {version})

What the import does:
The Library is the backbone of citation: it holds ONLY sources — works ("work"), quotes ("quote") and people as authors ("person"); a library entry points only to other library entries (a quote → its work, a work → authors, translators, the book or periodical it is in). Your own texts (sermons, talks, articles) are in the Scriptorium (format "{scriptorium}"), and knowledge — comments, people, places, events — in Knowledge (Cogita), as your own kinds; both cite from here. There are no topics.
- Every entry is { "id", "kind", "key", "data" }. An entry with an id from an export (or with the key of an existing entry of the same kind) is CHANGED — only the fields given in "data"; fields that are missing stay. To clear a field, give null.
- An entry without an id (or with an unknown one) is created new. The import deletes nothing.
- References ("authors", "editors", "translators", "container", "work"; for music "composers", "lyricists", "arrangers", "performers", "piece", "album") can be ids or keys: "@ratzinger2007". Keys from the same document work too — you can describe a whole library without knowing any id.
- Music is also works ("work"), with another type: "piece" (piece), "score" (sheet music), "recording" (recording), "album" (album). The type decides which fields the work has. Sheet music and a recording point to their piece ("piece"), a recording — to its album ("album"). Files (pages of sheet music, tracks of a recording: separate voices and instruments or the whole) are uploaded in the app; JSON describes them without files or carries them from an export. A place in a recording is a time: "1:23", "1:23–1:45".
- A file with other kinds (texts, deliveries, projects, comments, topics) is rejected — with a note where to import it.
- "key" is the citation key: short, without spaces (e.g. "ratzinger2007"); texts refer to it as [@ratzinger2007, s. 23]. Omitted — one will be suggested.
- Numbers may have a unit ("384 s.", "20,5 cm"); a choice field accepts the value ("hard") or its name ("Twarda").
- Quotes from one book (e.g. read by AI from photos) have their own format "{quotes}" — they are imported on that book's page.
- Who sees an entry is decided only by the area of its library: the area's members, and when the area is public — everyone. There are no private fields and no publishing of single entries; what is to stay private goes to the library of a private area.
Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

{
  "format": "{format}",
  "version": {version},
  "name": "My library",
  "entries": [ { "kind": "person", "key": "ratzinger", "data": { … } }, … ]
}

## Kinds of entries
describe.use:
## How the app uses this data
- In the Library entries stand in the tabs “Sources”, “Music”, “Quotes” and “People”; each has its page, and “Map” draws the connections (quote → work → authors). The code scanner opens a book by "isbn" or by "libraryNumber".
- [@key, place] in a Scriptorium text, in a knowledge-base entry or in a page's “Text” module becomes a footnote (the first time a full description, then a short one); below a Scriptorium text and in print (LaTeX) there is a “Sources” list. ![@quote-key] inserts a quote as a block captioned with where it comes from.
- Texts store the entry's id, not its description: corrected data of a work or person shows at once in every footnote, and changing a key breaks nothing.
- The page module “Quote collection” shows the quotes of this library (or of one work): a “thought of the day” or a collection with search.
- A knowledge base that has this library among its sources points to its entries, and card templates and reviews can use them (e.g. quotes); nothing is copied. In the Scriptorium a text type can have a field that points to a work with a place (e.g. "@bt" and "Łk 1,26-38").
- “Connections” on an entry show what points to it — in libraries, scriptoria and knowledge bases the reader can open.
- The full text of a work comes with a separate import (“Source text”, “Work with text”); then quoted places lead to the paragraph (“show in text”).
- Entries are sealed in the browser with the area key. “AI access” (an area link, MCP server), if it covers this library, gives the assistant a copy of it to read — the assistant searches and reads entries and changes nothing.

quotesDoc.head:
# Quotes of one book as JSON ("{format}", version {version})

What the import does (on the page of the book “{title}”):
- Every quote becomes a “Quote” entry with this book as its source; the citation key is assigned automatically ({key}-1, {key}-2, …).
- Before saving you see the list: every quote can be corrected or unticked.
- A quote already in this book (the same text) is unticked. A quote with an "id" from an export is changed in place.
- The quotes go to this book's library — whoever sees its area sees them. The library holds only sources: quotes have no topics or comments (your own thoughts are a kind in Knowledge).
- Older fields ("topics", "comment", "description", "notes") are only shown while checking — they are not saved.
- Nothing is deleted.
Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

{
  "format": "{format}",
  "version": {version},
  "work": {summary},
  "quotes": [ { … }, … ]
}

## Fields of a quote ("quotes": a list)
quotesDoc.afterFields:
"text" is required. Separate paragraphs in "text" with an empty line.

Example:
quotesDoc.use:
## How the app uses this data
- Quotes stand on the book's page (“Quotes from this book”) in the order of places in the work (pages as numbers, Holy Scripture by the canon) and in the library's “Quotes” tab.
- [@{key}] in a Scriptorium text or in a knowledge-base entry gives a footnote to this book with the quote's place; ![@{key}] inserts the whole quote as a block captioned with where it comes from (also as a plan point).
- The page module “Quote collection” shows the quotes of the library or of this book only: a “thought of the day” (different each day, the same for everyone) or a collection with search.
- When the reader can open the full text of this book and the quote's place is in it, “show in text” stands below the quote.
- A knowledge base that has this library among its sources can make cards and reviews from the quotes; nothing is copied. An entry in Knowledge that points to a quote (e.g. your own comment) shows at the quote under “Connections”.
- Quotes are sealed in the browser with the library's area key. “AI access” (an area link, MCP server), if it covers this library, gives the assistant the quotes to search and read; the assistant changes nothing.

quotesPrompt.marked: The reader marked passages in the book in pencil that they want to keep: underlining, vertical lines or brackets in the margin, exclamation marks, ticks. Transcribe EVERY marked passage as a separate quote. Do not transcribe unmarked text.
quotesPrompt.whole: Each photo shows a passage to keep. Transcribe the whole main text of each photo as a quote (without the running head, the page number and the footnotes at the bottom of the page).
quotesPrompt.intro: The photos show pages of the book: {book}.
quotesPrompt.rules:
Rules:
- Transcribe word for word, as printed: spelling, punctuation, quotation marks. Do not correct, summarise or translate anything.
- Join words hyphenated at the end of a line (“prayer-” + “ful” → “prayerful”). No line breaks inside a paragraph; separate paragraphs with an empty line.
- If a marking starts or ends in the middle of a sentence, transcribe exactly the marked range. Mark an omitted middle with “[…]”.
- A passage that runs onto the next page is ONE quote — "page": "23–24".
- Take the page number from the printed page number of that page. If it is not visible, leave "page" empty and set "uncertain": true.
- Transcribe a reader's handwritten note at the passage in "check" (the passage itself without the note).
- If you are not sure about a word or the edges of a marking: "uncertain": true and briefly in "check" what to check.
- Order of quotes: by page.
